items.prompt: Why can't anyone start on 'make checkout faster' on Monday morning?
choices: The checkout code is always too old to change
It names a goal but no specific piece to work on
Faster checkout is only possible after buying much more powerful hardware
items.explanation: A vague ask is too coarse to act on, not too hard; naming a piece makes it workable.

items.prompt: What is the first useful step toward 'make checkout faster'?
choices: Rewrite the whole checkout from scratch before looking at any numbers
Ask people to be more patient while paying
Measure where the 4.2 seconds actually goes
items.explanation: Splitting the time into named stages turns one vague ask into specific ones.

items.prompt: What does decomposition mean?
choices: Splitting a problem into smaller pieces that can each be worked on
Rewording one long sentence into shorter ones
Giving every person a copy of the whole problem
items.explanation: The pieces must be real sub-problems, not just a shorter way of saying the same thing.

items.prompt: You think 'I don't know where to start.' What does that usually signal?
choices: The problem is too hard to ever be solved
The problem has not been split into pieces yet
You should wait until more people join in
items.explanation: It is a cue to decompose, not a verdict on difficulty.

items.prompt: Which list best splits 'my morning is chaotic'?
choices: Being tired, being late, and being stressed out
Doing everything faster and more calmly from the moment the alarm rings
Waking up, getting ready, breakfast, finding keys, the bus
items.explanation: Good pieces are stages you can look at one by one, not moods or wishes.

items.prompt: After splitting, how do you know a fix to the lookup worked?
choices: The lookup's own time dropped from 2,500ms
Checkout feels faster to the developer who fixed it
The team agrees the new code looks cleaner now
items.explanation: Each piece has its own number, so progress can be measured directly.

items.prompt: Which of these can a person start on today?
choices: Make checkout better for everyone using it
Cut the data lookup from 2,500ms to under 500ms
Improve the overall experience of paying online
items.explanation: Only a specific, measurable piece is something you can begin today.

items.prompt: Network 300ms, server 800ms, lookup 2,500ms, drawing 600ms: what is the total?
items.explanation: 300 + 800 + 2,500 + 600 = 4,200, so the stages account for the whole.

items.prompt: Two requests land on a team: 'reduce signup drop-off' and 'cut the signup form's load time from 3 seconds to 1 second'. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The first is ready to assign because dropping off is the real business goal and everything else follows
The second is ready to assign because it names one measurable piece, while the first still needs splitting
Both are equally ready, since each of them is aimed at making signup work better for people
Neither is ready, because a request only becomes workable after the whole team has agreed on it
items.explanation: A ready task names a single piece with its own measure. The first request hides many possible causes.
items.reference:
From vague ask to workable piece
vague: 'make checkout faster' (4.2s)
split: network 300 / server 800 / lookup 2,500 / draw 600
workable: 'cut the lookup under 500ms'
Why: too coarse is not the same as too hard; naming and measuring the pieces makes the work startable.
items.learnMore:
Why a vague ask is not unsolvable

A request like 'make it faster' hides the pieces. Measuring and naming them gives each person something specific to do and a number to check afterwards.

Common mistake

Treating 'I don't know where to start' as proof the problem is too hard, when it only hasn't been split yet.

items.prompt: A team lead says a slow weekly report is 'too tangled to fix' and wants a rewrite. What is the best first move?
choices: Start the rewrite now, since a tangled report cannot be understood without replacing it
Ask every user which part of the report feels slowest and rewrite exactly that one
Time each stage from request to finished report, then see which stage dominates the total
Assign one engineer to each guess about the cause and pick whichever guess finishes first
items.explanation: A tangled feeling is the cue to measure and split; a rewrite before measuring may not touch the real cause.

Promise herself to move faster through every stage of the morning from now on
Buy a second watch so that she can see exactly how late she is each day

items.prompt: A problem was split into five clear pieces. What does that guarantee, and what does it not?
choices: Each piece is specific enough to act on, but the problem itself is not made easy
The problem is now easy, since five small tasks always take less effort than one big one
Every piece will matter equally, so the effort can safely be spread evenly across them
The solution is now known, because naming the pieces is the same as solving them all
items.explanation: Decomposition makes work actionable and measurable. The pieces can still be hard, and they rarely matter equally.

items.prompt: What does 'exhaustive' mean for a split?
choices: Every piece has exactly the same size
Each piece is owned by a different person
The pieces together cover the whole problem
items.explanation: If the pieces leave something out, a real cause hides outside the list.

items.prompt: What does 'non-overlapping' mean for a split?
choices: No two pieces describe the same cause
No two pieces may have the same number
Each piece must be fixed in a separate week
items.explanation: Overlap means counting one cause twice under two labels.

items.prompt: A trip takes 60 minutes. Pieces: walk 10, wait 20, bus 30. Is it exhaustive?
choices: No, because three pieces are never enough to describe a whole trip
Yes, because 10 + 20 + 30 equals 60
No, because the bus is longer than the walk
items.explanation: When the sum equals the measured total, nothing obvious is missing.

items.prompt: Pieces add up to more than the true total. What does that signal?
choices: Something is missing from the list
The total was measured on a different day
Something is being counted twice
items.explanation: A sum above the whole means at least one piece contains another.

items.prompt: Pieces add up to less than the true total. What does that signal?
choices: A contributor is missing from the list
Two pieces overlap each other
The pieces are perfectly independent
items.explanation: A shortfall means part of the problem is not named yet.

items.prompt: 'Total backend time' sits next to 'server processing' in one list. What is wrong?
choices: Backend time is always measured wrongly
One piece already contains the other
Server processing is too small to list
items.explanation: A superset next to its own part is a classic overlap.

items.prompt: Why does overlap make a fix look better than it is?
choices: Overlapping pieces are always the largest ones
Fixes only work when pieces are overlapping
Fixing one cause changes two pieces at once
items.explanation: The improvement shows up in both labels although only one cause changed.

items.prompt: Walk 10, wait 20, bus 30, 'commuting' 60. What is the sum?
choices: 120 minutes for a 60-minute trip
60 minutes for a 60-minute trip
90 minutes for a 60-minute trip
items.explanation: The 'commuting' piece contains the other three, so the sum doubles.

items.prompt: The stages of a 4,200ms checkout are listed as network 300ms, server 800ms and rendering 600ms. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The list is complete, because every stage that was named has been measured honestly
The list overlaps, because the three numbers are smaller than the measured total
About 2,500ms is unaccounted for, so a contributor is missing from the list
The list is fine as long as the three stages are worked on one at a time
items.explanation: 1,700ms of pieces against a 4,200ms whole leaves 2,500ms unnamed.
items.reference:
The two checks
exhaustive: do the pieces cover the whole?
non-overlapping: is each cause listed once?
sum equal / smaller / larger than the total
Why: a sum below the whole means a gap; a sum above it means double-counting.
items.learnMore:
Complete and not counted twice

Compare the sum of the pieces with an independently measured total. For problems without a total, ask whether the pieces cover the main reasons and whether any reason appears under two names.

Common mistake

Trusting a matching sum as proof, when an overlap and a gap can cancel each other out.
items.reflection: Think of a list of reasons you have written down for a problem. Do any two of them secretly describe the same cause?

items.prompt: A split of a 4,200ms checkout sums to 6,700ms because it lists 'server including lookup' (3,300ms) next to 'lookup' (2,500ms). What is the diagnosis?
choices: Missing piece: the 2,500ms excess is a stage nobody has measured yet
Measurement noise: stage timings always differ a little from the whole
Independence: the two pieces can be worked on at the same time safely
Overlap: the lookup is counted inside one piece and again on its own
items.explanation: The excess equals a piece that sits inside another one; the sum above the total points to double-counting.

It proves the split is sound, since matching totals leave no way for errors to hide
It proves the pieces are independent, since matching totals mean none depend on others
It proves nothing at all, since totals can never be compared with a sum of pieces
items.explanation: Equal sums are necessary evidence, not proof; also ask whether any single cause appears twice.

items.prompt: Customers who leave are explained by 'price too high', 'too expensive', 'slow delivery' and 'poor support'. What is wrong with the split?

The first two are the same cause under two labels, so the split overlaps
Delivery and support can't be compared with price, so they must be separate lists
Nothing is wrong, because each reason uses different words from the others
items.explanation: Different words do not make different causes; check the cause, not the wording.

items.prompt: What does 'independent' mean for a piece?
choices: It can be worked on without first solving the others
It can never affect any other piece
It is always the smallest piece in the list
items.explanation: Independent means workable and measurable by itself.

items.prompt: Which pair of pieces fails independence?
choices: Data lookup and screen drawing
Server-side time and end-to-end time
Network time and screen drawing, which can be changed separately
items.explanation: End-to-end time is partly made of server-side time.

items.prompt: The lookup is 2,500ms of a 4,200ms total. About what share is it?
choices: About 7%
About 19%
About 59%
items.explanation: 2,500 divided by 4,200 is roughly 0.595.

items.prompt: Network is 300ms of a 4,200ms total. About what share is it?
choices: About 7%
About 59%
About 19%
items.explanation: 300 divided by 4,200 is roughly 0.071.

items.prompt: Why does a split help with choosing where to work?
choices: It makes every piece equally important
The sizes of the pieces become visible
It removes the need to measure anything
items.explanation: Once pieces have numbers, the largest ones stand out.

items.prompt: Which piece would you look at first in checkout's split?
choices: The network at 300ms
The drawing at 600ms
The data lookup at 2,500ms
items.explanation: It is the biggest share, so changing it moves the total most.

items.prompt: Three equal pieces, none dominant. Is decomposition still useful?
choices: Yes, it still turns one vague problem into three workable ones
No, it only helps when one piece dominates
No, it works only for things measured in milliseconds
items.explanation: Splitting makes work specific even when the ranking is a tie.

items.prompt: What does the share of a piece tell you?
choices: How much the fix will cost to build
How far the total could move if that piece shrank
How many people should work on it
items.explanation: Share measures potential impact, not effort.

items.prompt: A split has pieces at 60%, 20%, 12% and 8% of the total. The 60% piece would take a quarter of a year to fix; the 20% piece takes a day. What does the decomposition itself tell you?
choices: That the 60% piece must be fixed first, since the largest share always wins
That the 20% piece must be fixed first, since quick fixes always win
That the effort should be split evenly among all four pieces in the list
How far each fix could move the total; the cost comparison needs separate judgment
items.explanation: Share measures potential gain. Whether to pay the price is a separate call.
items.reference:
Share tells you potential impact
lookup 2,500 / 4,200 = about 59%
network 300 / 4,200 = about 7%
after lookup falls to 500: server 800 / 2,200 = about 36%
Why: shares show where the total can move; they change as soon as one piece is fixed.
items.learnMore:
Independence and priority

A piece is independent when someone can measure it and test an idea on it without solving the others first. Once pieces are independent, their shares rank the potential gain of working on each.

Common mistake

Fixing the biggest piece forever; after each fix the shares change and the target may move.
items.reflection: Pick a chore or project you are juggling. Which piece is largest, and does it also happen to be the one you are avoiding?

items.prompt: Someone splits a slow report into 'reduce server-side time' and 'reduce end-to-end time'. What is the main problem?
choices: The second piece includes the first, so it is not workable alone
The pieces overlap in wording but each can still be fixed without the other
The pieces are too small, so they will not move the total in a visible way
The pieces are fine, because each one names a number someone can measure
items.explanation: A piece that is partly made of another can't be worked on without understanding the other first.

items.prompt: In 'our onboarding is confusing', is there a single total to add up?
choices: Yes, because every problem has a total that can be added up
No, so completeness is argued from causes and evidence
Yes, but only when it is measured in milliseconds
items.explanation: Not every problem is a sum of times.

items.prompt: What is a hypothesis table in this unit?
choices: A list of reasons to avoid measuring anything
A single total with the pieces added together
Steps with evidence, a possible cause, and what to check next
items.explanation: It organizes guesses so each can be checked.

items.prompt: Which column tells you how to test a guess?
choices: Check next
Who is affected
Step
items.explanation: 'Check next' names the cheapest way to confirm or reject the cause.

items.prompt: Splitting 'confusing' into new users and returning users may hide what?
choices: A cause that affects nobody at all
One cause shared by both groups
The total number of users
items.explanation: If one button confuses everyone, splitting by audience counts it twice.

items.prompt: Which split avoids repeating a cause more reliably?
choices: Splitting by the mood of each user
Splitting by the name of each team
Splitting by step of the journey
items.explanation: Journey steps are separate places, so causes don't repeat as easily.

items.prompt: Is the checkout example a typical or an easy case?
choices: An easy case, because the stages are measurable and add up
A hard case, because it needs the most guessing and the least measuring
A typical case, because every problem adds up to a total
items.explanation: Most real splits need judgment to check the same two properties.

items.prompt: What two questions still apply to a non-additive split?
choices: Is it short enough, and is it written clearly?
Does it cover the whole, and is each cause named once?
Is it fast enough, and is it cheap enough?
items.explanation: The same exhaustive and non-overlapping questions carry over.

items.prompt: A row says 'Profile setup: many abandoned forms'. What is it missing to be actionable?
choices: A longer description of the form
A different name for the step
A possible cause and a way to check it
items.explanation: Evidence alone says where the pain is, not what to try.

items.prompt: 'Our onboarding is confusing' is split into 'confusing for new users' and 'confusing for returning users'. Support finds one ambiguous button label behind both. What does this show?
choices: The audience split counted one cause twice, so splitting by journey step fits better
The split was exhaustive, since both groups of users have now been accounted for
The split was fine, because users with different histories always need two fixes
The split needs a third group, since two groups cannot cover every possible user
items.explanation: Splitting by who is affected can repeat a cause; splitting by where it happens exposes it.

add the pieces: not possible
cover the whole journey, name each cause once
evidence + possible cause + check next

Decomposition beyond sums

Common mistake

Splitting by audience when the real cause is shared across audiences.

items.prompt: Implement `totalMs(stages)`. `stages` is an array of `{ name, ms }`. Return the sum of every stage's `ms`.
items.explanation: Adding every stage's time gives the sum that a decomposition is compared against.

items.prompt: Implement `shareOf(stages, name)`. Return the named stage's `ms` divided by the total of all stages.
items.explanation: A share is one piece's time over the whole.

items.prompt: Implement `largestStage(stages)`. Return the `name` of the stage with the biggest `ms`.
items.explanation: The biggest piece is the first place to look.

items.prompt: Implement `isComplete(stages, measuredTotal)`. Return `true` when the stages' `ms` sum equals `measuredTotal`, otherwise `false`.
items.explanation: Equal sum and measured total is the basic completeness check.

items.prompt: Implement `hasOverlap(stages, measuredTotal)`. Return `true` when the stages' sum is greater than `measuredTotal`.
items.explanation: A sum above the whole means something is counted twice.

items.prompt: Implement `unaccountedMs(stages, measuredTotal)`. Return `measuredTotal` minus the sum of the stages' `ms`.
items.explanation: The gap is how much of the whole no piece explains.

items.prompt: Implement `stageNames(stages)`. Return an array of the stages' `name` values, in the same order.
items.explanation: Listing the pieces by name is the first step of any split.

items.prompt: Implement `smallestStage(stages)`. Return the `name` of the stage with the smallest `ms`.
items.explanation: The smallest piece is usually the least worth attention.

items.prompt: Implement `audit(stages, measuredTotal)`. Sum the stages' `ms`. Return `"complete"` if the sum equals `measuredTotal`, `"missing"` if it is smaller, and `"overlap"` if it is larger.

tests.expr: expect(audit([{ name: "network", ms: 300 }, { name: "server", ms: 800 }, { name: "db", ms: 2500 }, { name: "render", ms: 600 }], 4200)).toBe("complete")
expect(audit([{ name: "network", ms: 300 }, { name: "server", ms: 800 }, { name: "db", ms: 2500 }, { name: "render", ms: 600 }], 5000)).toBe("missing")
expect(audit([{ name: "network", ms: 300 }, { name: "server", ms: 800 }, { name: "db", ms: 2500 }, { name: "render", ms: 600 }], 3000)).toBe("overlap")

items.explanation: Comparing the sum with an independent total gives three verdicts. A smaller sum means a gap and a larger one means double-counting.

Auditing a split

Add the pieces and compare with an independently measured total. The verdict comes from the difference, and the biggest piece is found by comparing shares after any fix, since the bottleneck can move.

items.prompt: Implement `auditReport(stages, measuredTotal)`. Return an object `{ status, gapMs }` in that key order. `gapMs` is `measuredTotal` minus the stages' sum (negative when the stages overshoot). `status` is `"complete"` when the gap is 0, `"missing"` when it is positive, `"overlap"` when it is negative.

tests.expr: expect(auditReport([{ name: "network", ms: 300 }, { name: "server", ms: 800 }, { name: "db", ms: 2500 }, { name: "render", ms: 600 }], 4200)).toEqual({ status: "complete", gapMs: 0 })
expect(auditReport([{ name: "network", ms: 300 }, { name: "server", ms: 800 }, { name: "db", ms: 2500 }, { name: "render", ms: 600 }], 5000)).toEqual({ status: "missing", gapMs: 800 })
expect(auditReport([{ name: "network", ms: 300 }, { name: "server", ms: 800 }, { name: "db", ms: 2500 }, { name: "render", ms: 600 }], 4000)).toEqual({ status: "overlap", gapMs: -200 })
